name: Tangier
tagline: Where Africa looks across at Europe
intro: Phoenician traders, Romans, Portuguese, English and a whole committee of foreign powers have all held this port on the Strait of Gibraltar. Its history is a tug-of-war between two continents — and you can still see both from the Kasbah walls.

lessons.title: A square named after a speech
lessons.hook: The Grand Socco is where the medina meets the new town: buses, cafés, palm trees and the gate into the old city. Look around the square for its official name.
lessons.challenge: The square's official name is a date. Which date?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player gives 9 April 1947 in any format or language, or at least the year 1947.
hints: Look for the name on street signs or the marble monument in the square.
It's a day in spring, just after the Second World War.
lessons.story: On 9 April 1947, Sultan Mohammed V came to Tangier — then an international zone run by foreign powers — and gave a speech calling for Morocco's independence and unity. Crowds packed the Grand Socco, and the square was later renamed after that day. Nine years later Morocco was independent, and in 1956 Tangier rejoined it.

lessons.title: America's oldest home abroad
lessons.hook: Down a narrow lane in the lower medina stands a building with a very unexpected owner — look for the flag and the plaque by the door.
lessons.challenge: Which country has owned this building since 1821?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player names the United States / America.
hints: Look at the flag and the plaque at the entrance.
It's a country across the Atlantic that was only a few decades old in 1821.
lessons.story: In 1821 Sultan Moulay Suliman gave this building to the United States. It was the first property the US government ever acquired for a diplomatic mission, and it is still the only US National Historic Landmark in a foreign country. The friendship is older still: Morocco was among the very first countries to recognise the young United States, in 1777. Today it's a museum and cultural centre.

sources.label: 1821: Sultan Moulay Slimane gives the Legation to the US — TALIM

lessons.title: The palace on the cliff
lessons.hook: Climb to the top of the medina and through the Kasbah gate to the old sultan's palace. Find a spot on the walls with a view to the north.
lessons.challenge: Across the water you can see another country — on another continent. Which one?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says Spain (or Europe / the Spanish coast).
hints: Look north, across the Strait of Gibraltar.
On a clear day you can see the mountains of Andalusia.
lessons.story: England held Tangier from 1662 — it came as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry — and when the English left in 1684 they blew up their fortifications. Moroccan rulers built a new kasbah, and the Dar el Makhzen palace rose on the ruins of the English 'Upper Castle'. Today it's the Kasbah Museum. The strait below is only about 14 km wide at its narrowest, which is exactly why so many empires wanted this hill.

lessons.title: The Interzone
lessons.hook: Sit for a moment in the little café square in the heart of the medina. Seventy years ago, spies, smugglers and writers sat at these same tables.
lessons.challenge: From the 1920s until 1956 Tangier wasn't ruled by one country but by several together. What was this arrangement called?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says the International Zone (or Interzone, or an internationally governed city).
hints: Several foreign powers shared the job of running the city.
William Burroughs gave it a nickname that starts with 'Inter-'.
lessons.story: For about three decades Tangier was the Tangier International Zone, governed jointly by foreign powers. Low taxes and loose rules drew bankers, smugglers and spies — and writers. Paul Bowles settled here in 1947, and William S. Burroughs, who called the city 'Interzone', followed in the 1950s. The cafés of the Petit Socco were their meeting place. The zone ended in 1956, when Tangier rejoined independent Morocco.

sources.label: The International Zone: Expat Writers in Tangier — Culture Trip

lessons.title: Graves cut into the cliff
lessons.hook: On the clifftop at Marshan, west of the Kasbah, there are strange rectangular hollows cut into the rock, facing the sea.
lessons.challenge: What are those hollows carved into the rock?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says they are tombs / graves / burials.
hints: They're about the size and shape of a person lying down.
This was a place for the dead.
lessons.story: These are ancient tombs, cut into the rock more than two thousand years ago — around a hundred of them. Tangier began as a Phoenician trading post, Tingis, probably by the 8th century BC, and later became part of the Roman world. Its people buried their dead here, looking out over the strait that made the city rich.

lessons.title: The man who walked the world
lessons.place: Tomb of Ibn Battuta, Kasbah quarter
lessons.hook: In the lanes below the Kasbah, on a street that carries his name, is a small tomb said to belong to Tangier's most famous son.
lessons.challenge: He left Tangier in 1325, aged 21, and travelled for nearly 30 years. What is his name?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player names Ibn Battuta (any spelling).
hints: Read the street sign on the lane.
lessons.story: Ibn Battuta was born here in 1304. He set out on the pilgrimage to Mecca and simply kept going — across North Africa, the Middle East, India, China and al-Andalus — covering more ground than any traveller before him. Back in Morocco he dictated his journeys to the scholar Ibn Juzayy; the book is known as the Rihla. Nobody can prove he is really buried in this tomb, but it keeps his memory alive in his home town.

sources.label: Tomb of Ibn Battuta — Lonely Planet

lessons.title: A Spanish theatre in Morocco
lessons.hook: Walk down into the new town and find a large theatre with a decorated front — built when Tangier was home to thousands of Spanish families.
lessons.challenge: The theatre is named after Spain's most famous writer. Who?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player names Miguel de Cervantes.
hints: The name is written on the building.
lessons.story: The Gran Teatro Cervantes opened in 1913, when Tangier had a large Spanish community, and performers from across Europe played here. In 1928 its owners gave it to the Spanish state. After decades of decay Spain handed it to Morocco in 2023, and restoration has been bringing it back to life.

sources.label: Morocco recovers the Gran Teatro Cervantes — Atalayar
